registers.role: controls and subgroup definitions (occupation, firm, experience, education, children)

linkages: tax register records merged with IDA for every person in Denmark
individuals linked to spouses via spouse ID in the tax register (used for spousal deductions and the household-based middle tax base)
workers linked to occupations via four-digit ISCO codes in IDA; occupation-year cells used for modes and for aggregate/individual bunching by occupation

sample.universe: individuals aged 15-70 in the Danish population, 1994-2001 (the tax register contains records for more than 99.9% of them)
selection_rules: wage earners, excluding the self-employed and pensioners (analysis sample of 17.9 million observations)
much of the analysis uses the subset of wage earners within DKr 50,000 of the top tax cutoff (6.8 million observations)
self-employed individuals (positive self-employment income, 1.8 million observations) are studied separately as a comparison group
bunching figures bin recentred income in DKr 1,000 bins over the window of DKr 50,000 on each side of the kink
sample.n_observations: 30,492,819 person-years in the full population; 17,866,090 wage earners; 6,788,235 wage earners within DKr 50,000 of the top tax cutoff; 1,846,064 self-employed (Table I)

construction_notes: All monetary values are in real 2000 Danish Kroner; $1 is approximately DKr 6.
'Taxable income' means the tax base relevant to the particular tax studied (top tax base or middle tax base), not the Danish technical concept of Taxable Income.
Net deductions are defined as deductions minus non-wage income (accounting for spousal deductions), equivalently wage earnings minus taxable income.
Income is recentred on the year-specific bracket cutoff and grouped into DKr 1,000 bins over -50,000 to +50,000.
The counterfactual density is a seventh-degree polynomial (q = 7) fitted excluding bins within DKr 7,500 of the kink (R = 7), iterated to satisfy the integration constraint (equations (14)-(16)).

Standard errors for the excess mass b come from a parametric bootstrap that resamples the residuals of equation (15); they reflect misspecification of the counterfactual polynomial rather than sampling error.
The tax simulator predicts actual tax liabilities within DKr 5 for 95% of individuals; marginal tax rates are computed at the individual level, holding spouse income fixed.

Table II uses two-year differences: the dependent variable is the log change in real wage earnings between t-2 and t, and the regressor is the log change in the net-of-tax rate over the same interval, instrumented with the simulated change holding base-year characteristics fixed.
Occupation-level modes are the DKr 5,000 wage-earnings bin with the most individuals in an occupation-year cell (four-digit ISCO), excluding occupation-years with fewer than 7,000 workers.

treatment.label: the kink at the top tax bracket cutoff, where the net-of-tax wage rate falls by approximately 30%

register_source.value: Danish tax register (Statistics Denmark), 1994-2001; marginal tax rates from the authors' tax simulator

definition.value: The discrete fall of approximately 30% in the marginal net-of-tax wage rate at the top tax bracket cutoff (marginal tax rate rising to approximately 63%); taxable income for the top tax base is recentred on the year-specific top tax cutoff and grouped into DKr 1,000 bins. timing.value: measured in the year of observation, pooled over 1994-2001

outcome.label: Excess mass (b) at the kink in the distribution of taxable income (as defined for the relevant tax base)

register_source.value: Danish tax register (Statistics Denmark), 1994-2001; marginal tax rates from the authors' tax simulator

definition.value: Bunching in the taxable income distribution: the empirical histogram of taxable income relative to the bracket cutoff in DKr 1,000 bins. key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the jump in tax rates at the cutoff the income distribution would be smooth there, so the excess mass measured against the fitted counterfactual density is caused by the kink
key_assumptions.supported_by: the excess mass follows the top bracket cutoff as it moves across years rather than inflation or average wage growth (Figures IV and V); placebo tests at deduction thresholds from -20,000 to 40,000 find no bunching anywhere except the statutory and pension kinks

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density is well approximated by a seventh-degree polynomial fitted to the bin counts excluding bins within DKr 7,500 of the kink, shifted up to the right of the kink to satisfy the integration constraint
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors report that the qualitative results are not sensitive to the choice of q and R or to the way the integration constraint is imposed; at the middle kink the estimated excess mass converges to zero as the polynomial degree rises

key_assumptions.assumption: Translating the excess mass b into an observed elasticity uses Saez's (2010) approximation that the earnings density is uniform around the kink and that behaviour follows the iso-elastic labour supply model of equation (6)

threats_discussed: income shifting into tax-deductible pension contributions or capital income rather than real labour supply responses
tax evasion (argued away by third-party reporting of wage earnings)
shifting into unobservable non-taxable compensation such as office amenities, and intertemporal shifting, which the authors say they cannot rule out
heterogeneity in elasticities by income level or tax rate as an alternative to adjustment costs
endogenous sample selection from dropping the self-employed
robustness_checks: varying the polynomial degree q and the excluded window R, and the way the integration constraint is imposed
tracking the excess mass as the top bracket cutoff moves across years (Figures IV and V)
adding employer and employee pension contributions back into taxable income (Figure A.2)
switchers between the top and middle kinks, which removes individual fixed effects (Figure A.3)
restricting to higher earners in a couple or singles, to address jointness of the middle tax (Figure A.4)
excluding households with at least one self-employed person
unresolved_confounders: substitution of compensation into unobservable nontaxable forms, e.g. office amenities
intertemporal shifting of wage earnings to avoid paying the top tax
